items.title: Inside the early GOP reckoning after historic defeat
items.standfirst: Stephen Miller's rise to chief of staff exacerbated GOP fears that there will be no party-wide reckoning after their midterm wipeout.
items.content: President Donald Trump's decision to name hard-line loyalist Stephen Miller as his top aide cemented what many Republicans were already privately fearing: There will be no party-wide GOP reckoning with this week's midterm bloodbath.Instead, with Trump still in office for another two years, most have grown resigned to the reality that the president is going to lean in on a confrontational approach with Congress — and is not willing to change course.Republicans on Capitol Hill and inside the Trump administration are questioning how and whether they can break with the president now after having green-lit much of his agenda, according to more than a dozen GOP lawmakers, senior aides and Trump officials interviewed for this story, some of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the party’s future.Trump's decision Friday to elevate Miller, the architect of his unpopular mass deportation policy and an advocate of fierce partisan confrontation, crystallized the frustration.“There needs to be some self-reflection for Republicans,” Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) said in an interview about the midterm losses Friday morning. “There should be some heads rolling at the White House because we lost badly.”Hours later, heads did roll. Trump announced Miller would replace Susie Wiles as his new chief of staff.“Horrible decision,” Stutzman said in response.One House Republican, when informed that Trump had named Miller his chief of staff, replied: “Please tell me you’re lying to me right now, just to get a reaction.”The immediate aftermath of the election has sharpened the GOP’s core issue for the past decade: They are struggling to navigate the man who they reshaped their entire identity around, and whose record low approval with voters helped to fuel generational losses within the party.The Iran war is another area where some Republicans are having regrets. Vice President JD Vance identified it as the main reason for the party’s defeat in his election post-mortem.The problem with Vance’s assessment, one senior Hill Republican said, is, “we’ve been fucking voting for the war since March — because they told us to.”Republicans and Trump advisers expect the president to wield massive influence in the 2028 GOP primaries, another reason many are staying quiet."Everyone is staring at each other and wondering who will speak up and blame Trump first," said one GOP operative who worked on a battleground race Democrats won. They, like others in this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. "But we've been here before. I'm not holding my breath. He still controls the party and its primaries, at least for now." The White House responded to POLITICO's request for comment by referring to Trump's praise for Miller on Friday. The RNC declined to comment.Miller wrote on social media that he is "honored beyond words to serve as [Trump's] White House Chief of Staff" and "the mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President."How much lawmakers will distance themselves will be put to the test quickly: House Republicans will have an immediate opportunity to break with Trump and the war next week, when Rep. Thomas Massie said in an interview with POLITICO he will trigger his articles of impeachment against Secretary Pete Hegseth. “There are a lot of questions about Hegseth,” House Oversight Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) said Friday.Some senior Republicans are privately nudging Trump officials to ditch Hegseth before the vote, according to two people with direct knowledge of the conversations. The White House is sticking by Hegseth so far, however.House Republicans will also have a chance to elect new leadership next week, including a new chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee. But in a sign of what’s to come, none of the candidates — including Reps. Brian Jack (R-Ga.) and Rudy Yakym (R-Ind.) — nor any other GOP leadership candidates have publicly suggested doing more to break with Trump.A small group of Republicans on Capitol Hill have privately declared, as of Tuesday night, that “MAGA is over,” and it’s time for a “reset,” as one House GOP aide put it — and yet it’s a sentiment no prominent Republican is willing to say publicly.Rep. Chris Smith (R-N.J.), one of the longest-serving members of the House, said he wasn’t going to “blame” others for Tuesday’s losses, which left him as the sole GOP incumbent survivor in his home state. Asked if Republicans were dragged down by the president, Smith replied: “I don’t want to answer that.”Rep. Warren Davidson (R-Ohio) went a step further. He declined to name Trump, but he said in an interview that he was tired of GOP leaders “ignoring” voters — a remarkable position for a party that Trump transformed into a working-class coalition."We had a lot of Republican leaders out there saying ‘everything's fine.’ And you kind of had the boomer generation saying, 'Well, yeah, back in my day, interest rates were 15%, so everything's good,’” said Davidson, a 56-year-old former Army Ranger. “Well, you had a lot of hardworking young people who felt really ignored, and they they went to the polls and said, 'Stop ignoring us.'"Davidson said Republicans need to start discussing their problems quickly, or suffer the electoral consequences again."Bad news doesn't get better with time. So avoiding talking about something doesn't solve the problem," he said. He said Vance “walked a pretty good line” by being “candid” in his election post-mortem Wednesday.Vance and other potential 2028 presidential contenders like Sen. Ted Cruz don’t have much time to waste if they want to chart a new path away from Trump. Cruz issued his own post-mortem that included a call to focus more on voters’ economic concerns. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said “this midterm was a rebuke of the president and Congress.”French Hill, the powerful Financial Services Committee Chair who narrowly survived a strong Democratic challenge in his own deep-red Arkansas seat Tuesday night, pointed to “President Trump’s unfavorability” which hit “races across the country.” Hill added: “He will be considered a lame duck, and that often has members of both political parties looking out at who will be the standard-bearers in the 2028 presidential election.”Most others have remained silent in public.One thing is certain: The utter devastation in deep-red seats is stirring deep anger among many Hill Republicans, who believe something needs to change.It’s fueling private recriminations at Trump’s political operation that his advisers didn’t take early warnings seriously about the extent of the damage in states like North Carolina. Trump’s now-former chief of staff Susie Wiles will join his political operation, the president announced Friday.Trump's team has blamed "candidate quality" for the losses, instead of the president himself.“Candidate quality matters. Unless you’re running for the U.S. Senate. They apparently don’t care if you would lose to a pinecone,” said a House Republican, referring to Trump's hand-picked North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley.The National Republican Senatorial Committee declined to comment.Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), who leads the Senate campaign arm and saw Democrats flip a Senate seat in his own state, did not answer reporters’ questions on Thursday. The South Carolina Republican has a policy of not talking to reporters in the halls — and he didn’t start when POLITICO and others asked why Republicans lost so badly.Back in August, some Republicans in seats Trump won by double digits were already telling the White House to keep the president away from their districts. Others publicly broke from the White House on mass deportations and the Iran war.NRCC Chair Richard Hudson had largely dismissed those concerns when POLITICO asked him in a hallway interview on Sept. 1.“Based on our polling, the president's a net positive in every district. And I've been encouraging him to get out and do events and do rallies. I'm going to continue to do that,” Hudson said. “I think the more he talks about his record and incredible achievements he's made over the last Congress, I think the better.”Then, Hudson lost his own reelection bid. He is the first ever NRCC chair in history to be defeated in a general election.Mia McCarthy, Andrew Howard and Samuel Benson contributed to this report.

items.title: Stephen Miller to Be Trump's New Chief of Staff, Replacing Susie Wiles
items.standfirst: Miller has been the driving force behind Trump's immigration agenda.
items.content: Stephen Miller, center, sits behind Susie Wiles, left, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer at a bilateral meeting at U.N. Headquarters on Sept. 22, 2026 in New York City. —Chip Somodevilla—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Friday announced Stephen Miller will be the next White House Chief of Staff starting Monday, the most high-profile shift in his Administration in the aftermath of midterm elections on Tuesday in which Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress.Susie Wiles, the current White House Chief of Staff and Trump’s longtime political operative, will be reassigned to oversee “the Trump Political Operation,” according to Trump’s Truth Social Post. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!” Trump said. Read more: Welcome to Trump’s Lame-Duck EraSpeaking to reporters Friday afternoon, Trump praised Miller as "a great manager" and "very good politically and a very good man."“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning," he said. "He gets it."Wiles, 69, was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year and underwent six months of chemotherapy while continuing to manage her duties in the White House. In September, Wiles announced that she is cancer-free after the pathology results came back. In a statement posted on X, Wiles says it has been “an honor of a lifetime” to serve President Trump in the White House and she is grateful for the people that have worked alongside her.“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she said. Miller has served as White House Deputy Chief of Staff in Trump’s second term, and is considered to be the central figure of Trump’s immigration agenda, including mass deportations and closing the US-Mexico border. Miller has overseen Trump’s homeland security agenda along with border czar Tom Homan. He previously served as senior advisor to the president and director of speechwriting during the first Trump administration. During that period, Miller, along with then White House Strategist Steve Bannon, co-wrote the Muslim ban and encouraged Trump to gradually end the recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, also known as DACA.Miller’s promotion quickly drew backlash from Democrats in Congress who have vowed to investigate the Trump Administration following a sweeping midterm victory. Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said in a statement that Stephen Miller should “lawyer up.”“Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts,” Garcia added.

items.title: What to Know About Gavin Newsom’s Historic Commutation of All California Death Sentences
items.standfirst: It’s the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history, drawing sharp reactions and potential legal questions.
items.content: Governor of California Gavin Newsom is seen at 'Jimmy Kimmel Live!' in Los Angeles, Calif., on Oct. 28, 2026. —PG/Bauer-Griffin—Getty ImagesCalifornia Gov. Gavin Newsom has moved to grant clemency to all 548 people on death row in the state, marking the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history.In an open letter to Californians on Thursday, Newsom said he would commute the sentence of every death row inmate to life in prison without the possibility of parole—“the most severe punishment I can lawfully impose and the state of California can ethically enforce.”“Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing,” Newsom, a Democrat, wrote.California holds the largest number of people on death row in the U.S. and the western hemisphere. Newsom’s action, if fully enforced, would commute a quarter of all death sentences in the country. It takes a step beyond the moratorium that has been in place since Newsom first became governor in 2019. Newsom’s successor, Democrat Xavier Becerra, has also committed to a stay on carrying out executions.Opponents to the death penalty welcomed the move, arguing that it is consequential to the broader movement to abolish the death penalty. Supporters of the death penalty, including some groups representing victims of crime and their families, have argued that the action disregards individual judgments reached by courts and the feelings of victims’ families.The state last executed a person in 2006 under the governorship of Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger.The move will be among Newsom’s final actions before he leaves office in January. He is expected to announce a 2028 presidential run, which some argue Thursday’s action could impact, for better or for worse.The question of capital punishment has received heightened scrutiny in the U.S. since Tennessee botched the execution of Christa Pike at the end of September, which led her to be hospitalized for days before returning to prison. On Thursday, Alabama, Florida, and Indiana carried out executions by lethal injection. And the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan at Fort Hood also drew national attention after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in October that the execution would be live-streamed. President Donald Trump has since scrapped that live-streaming plan, but the military execution by firing squad is still planned for December.‘Incompatible’ with justiceA Catholic who has long opposed the death penalty on moral grounds, Newsom said Thursday that the state’s system for administering the death penalty cannot be applied fairly and has resulted in wrongful convictions.“Because the death penalty is inherently incompatible with our legal system’s commitment to justice, I have determined that this clemency decision, while difficult in many respects, will ultimately affirm the strength and integrity of our state and its justice system,” he wrote.Newsom has taken actions against the death penalty before. He dismantled the execution chamber at San Quentin in 2019 and the next year began transferring its death row inmates into the general population at other secure prisons where they had more access to work and restitution opportunities while remaining under death sentences. Newsom later converted the facility into a rehabilitation center, and in February, he opened a new Learning Center expanding education, training, and reentry services.On an episode of Newsom’s podcast last month that featured Equal Justice Initiative director Bryan Stevenson, the governor described the question of whether or not to grant universal clemency as a test of his conscience.The governor has long argued that the administration of the death penalty has been unequal. After announcing the moratorium on executions in 2019, Newsom said in an interview that he was responsible for addressing “a race-based system. The fact is, you’re better off in this country to be rich and guilty than if you’re poor and innocent.”According to the nonpartisan Death Penalty Information Center, at least 203 people on death row across 30 states have been exonerated based on evidence of innocence since 1973. That includes eight people in California.Elisabeth Semel, a professor of law at U.C. Berkeley and co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the university, tells TIME there exist “racial disparities in who faces capital punishment, who is sentenced to death, and who is executed” that trace back to the country’s history of slavery, segregation, and lynching.Black people accounted for a third of California’s death row population, despite making up around 6% of the state’s overall population, according to Judicial Council budget materials from May. Of those exonerated nationwide since 1973, 65% were people of color and more than half were Black. A 2017 analysis by the National Registry of Exonerations found that official misconduct contributed to the wrongful convictions of 87% of Black death row exonerees, compared to 67% of white death row exonerees. A 2024 study of California murder and manslaughter convictions between 1978 and 2002 also found that Black and Latino defendants were more likely to receive death sentences, even after accounting for culpability and statutory aggravating factors.Semel says most states do not provide adequate counsel or resources to people facing the death penalty. At the end of 2025, 391 people, or 70% of California’s death row population, were awaiting the appointment and/or funding of lawyers for state habeas corpus proceedings, according to a May 2026 report by the Habeas Corpus Resource Center.Death penalty opponents also argue that carrying out executions is a costly endeavor. Since 1978, when California reinstated the death penalty, the state has spent around $6 billion on the death penalty system while executing 13 men, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Many death penalty cases also involve lengthy legal battles, keeping people on death row for years and sometimes decades. Two-thirds of the people on death row in California were sentenced more than 20 years ago, according to the center.Some political analysts have warned that Newsom’s decision could expose him to criticism during a general election. While support for capital punishment in California and nationwide has declined since historical highs in the tough-on-crime eras of the mid-1980s and 1990s, the issue remains divisive. The death penalty remains legal in 27 states.But analysts also said that the move could boost Newsom’s popularity among progressive voters during a Democratic primary. “A governor who … predicts or precipitates capital punishment’s end in California could look visionary,” wrote David Carrillo, executive director at Berkeley Law’s California Constitution Center, and attorney Brandon Stracener last month.Shortly after Newsom’s announcement, three anti-death penalty groups sponsored a video advertisement praising Newsom’s decision, and comparing it to the actions of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Dolores Huerta, Robert F. Kennedy, and other notable social justice leaders.‘Mercy for the wolves’Newsom’s decision will not automatically commute the sentences of everyone on death row. While the governor has constitutional authority to grant clemency, cases involving a person with multiple felony convictions must be reviewed by the Supreme Court. That means that 382, or around 70%, of the 548 sentences Newsom seeks to commute will have to be reviewed.Even so, Semel tells TIME that the court’s role is “extremely limited.” The court is not meant to decide whether each applicant deserves mercy, but rather whether the governor’s action is an “abuse” of his broad constitutional authority, such as corruption or a conflict of interest, Semel says.The move will also likely face legal challenges, but Semel says lawsuits against similar moves in other states have not succeeded because the governor has broad authority to grant clemency.“The governor’s power of clemency under the California Constitution is almost without limit,” she says.Nevertheless, victims’ rights groups have raised both moral and legal objections to the move.The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF), which advocates for victims’ rights and public safety in state and federal courts, argued in a statement that the action overrides the decisions of juries that settled on verdicts and judges that handed down sentences. It also goes against the wishes of California voters, who twice rejected propositions to repeal the death penalty in 2012 and 2016, argued Anne Marie Schubert, a former Sacramento district attorney and the president and CEO of CJLF.In an op-ed published in the Los Angeles Times last month, Schubert, alongside El Dorado County district attorney Vern Pierson, argued that blanket commutation “substitutes an individual executive’s stance for those individual judgments.” Newsom is not the first governor to issue a blanket commutation: In 2003, Illinois Gov. George Ryan, a Republican, commuted 167 death sentences before leaving office—then the largest blanket grant of capital clemency. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, commuted all three remaining death sentences to life without parole in March 2020, the same day he signed legislation abolishing capital punishment.But Schubert and Pierson argued that clemency deserves individual review. “Clemency is a legitimate constitutional power. It can correct injustice or recognize circumstances warranting mercy,” they wrote. “But the authority to grant clemency carries a responsibility to exercise it wisely and justly. That requires examining each case on its merits, not treating hundreds of distinct judgments alike. How do we explain otherwise to the families we asked to trust the system?”Other California prosecutors also condemned Newsom’s action and said they intend to continue pursuing the death penalty where they deemed appropriate.“You cannot have crime without punishment,” Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer, a Republican, said in a statement on Thursday. Spitzer described Newsom’s action as “mercy for the wolves and while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep.”San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson accused Newsom of “political showmanship.”‘Expands the circle of pain’In his letter, Newsom acknowledged that some victims’ families would strongly disagree with his decision, which he said “will always weigh heavily” on him.“Some have said I should not grant clemency to people who committed the ‘worst of the worst’ crimes,” Newsom wrote. “I have learned, however, from speaking with the victims harmed by these crimes, that each experiences their loss as the worst of the worst. I have concluded that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims—those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.”Among those Newsom met with was Jess Nichol, whose stepsister Polly Klaas was kidnapped and murdered in 1993 at age 12. Nichol once believed in the death penalty, but said in a statement that “over time I’ve realized that whether he’s executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety.” She now helps facilitate rehabilitation and mediation programs at San Quentin.Klaas’s father, Marc Klaas, has opposed the commutations, describing Newsom’s decision as a “knife in the back” to victims’ families. Several other victims’ families had urged Newsom not to grant clemency, with some saying they were not given a chance to meet with him.Earlier this week, a group of 50 murder victims’ family members sent a letter to Newsom calling for blanket commutation.“The pain of losing a loved one through violence never goes away. The best we can hope for is some finality in the legal process so that we can begin healing,” the group wrote. “But for many victims’ families the death penalty prolongs an already agonizing experience with a lengthy process that leaves survivors with more pain, despair, and isolation.”Other opponents to the death penalty, including former prosecutors, former corrections officials, faith leaders, and civil rights groups, wrote similar letters urging universal clemency in the months preceding Thursday’s announcement.“As someone who has carried out executions in California, I am haunted by the fear that we will execute an innocent person,” Jeanne Woodford, a former warden at San Quentin who presided over four executions, said in a statement supporting Newsom’s decision.Semel, who has represented defendants in criminal cases for more than 50 years, including people facing capital punishment for more than 40, tells TIME that “all of my experiences have solidified my view that the death penalty reflects the worst in us.“It is ultimately an act of retribution that perpetuates violence and hatred and expands the circle of pain inflicted on loved ones beyond the grief victim family members endure to our clients’ families—their parents, siblings, and especially their children—and to us as a society.”
